data.copy:
I can usually predict which of my patients will end up with kidney disease years before any blood test can.

I don't need a lab for it. I just ask the owner one question during the checkup:

"When did you last actually see your cat drink?"

Most people go quiet. They have to think. A lot of them can't remember a single specific time. The bowl gets refilled, the level goes down a little, and everyone assumes things are fine.

That silence tells me more than the bloodwork does. Because in 12 years of running a feline-only practice in Pittsburgh, the pattern has never changed. The cats who quietly stop drinking are the cats whose kidneys I'm managing five years later. And by the time the bloodwork catches it, 75% of kidney function is already gone for good.

I'm Dr. Emily Parker, and I want to explain why your cat is almost certainly drinking less than you think, and what that's doing to her.

Here's the math I live with every week. One in three cats over age 7 develops kidney disease. By age 15 it's closer to 80%. Once the tissue is gone, it stays gone. There's no procedure, no medication, no diet that rebuilds a kidney. All veterinary medicine can offer is slowing down what's left of the decline.

Which means the whole game is prevention. And prevention comes down to one thing: water. A cat who stays properly hydrated keeps her kidneys. A cat who runs chronically dehydrated grinds hers down a little more every year.

So why can't you just fill a bowl and call it solved? I used to think you could. Then I started paying attention to why my "seems fine" patients kept showing up with failing kidneys, and I found four separate problems stacked on top of each other.

Start with biology. Cats descend from desert hunters. In the wild they got 70 to 80% of their water from the bodies of their prey, so evolution never bothered giving them a real thirst drive. Your cat doesn't feel thirsty until she's already dehydrated. A full bowl sitting out 24 hours a day doesn't fix a brai…

Nothing.

I was not doing that to my body for a toenail.

Vicks for six weeks. Tea tree oil twice a day for three months.

data.copy:
I'm a parasitologist. I've spent 12 years studying parasites that live inside the human body.
I am literally the person whose entire job is to find these organisms.
And in 12 years, not one doctor has ever called me first. I'm always the last phone call. After the IBS diagnosis. After the sleep medication. After the antidepressant. After years of suffering.
By then, it's years too late. And what I find under my microscope proves it.
—
Let me explain what "too late" looks like under 400x magnification.
I work in a university research lab affiliated with a major hospital system. Doctors send me samples when they've run out of answers. Biopsies. Tissue sections. Stool specimens from patients who've been sick for years and nobody can figure out why.
I prepare the slide. Saline wet mount. Iodine stain. Sometimes a trichrome stain for deeper tissue analysis. Standard parasitology procedure — far more thorough than anything a commercial lab performs.
I look through the eyepiece.
And there they are.
Eggs. Clusters of them. Oval-shaped, embedded deep in the tissue. Not floating loose on the surface. Embedded. Anchored into the mucosal lining like they were planted there.
Larvae. Some still moving. Tiny, pale, worm-like shapes that twist and curl even after being separated from the host.
And surrounding everything — this thick, grayish, gelatinous matrix that coats the tissue so completely it's sometimes hard to see the intestinal cells underneath.
Biofilm. The fortress wall.
Parasites build it around themselves to survive. It shields them from your immune system. It shields them from medications. It shields them from every diagnostic tool your doctor has access to.
I've seen biofilm so dense that I had to chemically dissolve it before I could even visualize the organisms hiding inside.
That's what "too late" looks like. That's what five, seven, ten years of missed diagnosis looks like on a slide.

data.copy:
Please STOP Taking Magnesium Until You Read This!
 
Because that bottle you bought? It's probably filled with something your body can't even absorb.
 
Let me explain.

Then I'd lie there for hours. Watching the ceiling. Calculating how exhausted I'd be tomorrow.
 
I was sleeping 3 to 5 hours a night. Broken. Restless. Awful.

I have been a veterinary dermatologist for 15 years and I am about to say something that every pharmaceutical rep who walks into my clinic would prefer I keep to myself.

The summer allergy protocol in veterinary medicine is designed to manage your dog's symptoms forever. It is not designed to fix the problem. And the difference between those two things is costing dog owners thousands of dollars a year while their dogs get worse.

I am done pretending that is acceptable.

My name is Dr. Katherine Mercer. I practice veterinary dermatology at Whitmore Animal Hospital. I have treated over 3,000 allergy patients in my career. And I need to tell you what I see every summer that nobody in this industry wants to talk about.

Every May I pull up my appointment schedule and I already know what it is going to look like. I can predict it almost to the day.

The dogs who were stable in winter are going to start deteriorating. The ones on Apoquel are going to need dose increases. The ones on Cytopoint are going to need their injection windows shortened. The ones who were "managed" in February are going to be scratching through the night by June.

And the owners are going to walk in and ask the same questions they asked last May. With a little more exhaustion in their voices. A little more resignation. A little less hope.

"Why is it worse this year?"

That is the question I get asked more than any other question in my career. And for the first ten years of my practice I gave the same inadequate answer every other vet gives.

"Seasonal allergies can fluctuate year to year. Some years the pollen count is higher. Some dogs become more sensitized over time."

That answer is not wrong. But it is incomplete to the point of being misleading. Because it implies the problem is external. That something in the environment is changing. That the dog is reacting to a variable outside its body.

The variable is not outside the dog.

The variable is inside the dog. And it has been changing ever…

data.copy:
If your cat's whiskers are getting shorter, thinner, or falling out at the root, you have 4-6 months before the next thing starts going.

Whiskers aren't decoration. They're keratin sensors anchored 3 times deeper than fur, and they're connected to one of the highest-density nerve clusters in your cat's body.

When whiskers start failing, it means the cat's body has run out of the building blocks to maintain them. And whiskers are usually the FIRST tissue to start losing those building blocks.

The next tissue is the heart muscle.

I learned that in a feline specialist's office 90 minutes from my house after three other vets told me my cat Theo's whisker loss was "totally normal."

By the time I got to her, Theo's whiskers were down to 16 from 24…

I found my cat's whisker on my pillow on a Tuesday in February. By the time three vets told me to stop worrying about it, my cat was 6 weeks away from permanent heart damage.

I'm writing this because if you've ever found a whisker on the floor, on the couch, on your pillow, on your shirt — and your vet told you it was "totally normal" — I need you to read every word of what's about to come next.

I almost lost my cat because every general vet I went to laughed me out of the exam room.

My name is Margaret. I'm 44. I live in Boulder with my husband and our cat Theo.

Theo is a 6-year-old orange tabby. He's the most loving cat I've ever had. He sits on my chest every morning at 6:15 sharp and pats my face with his paw until I open my eyes. He follows me from room to room. He sleeps on my pillow.

That's how I found the first whisker.

I woke up on a Tuesday in February, turned my head, and there was a long white whisker on the pillowcase. I picked it up. I held it between my fingers. I stared at it for what felt like a long time.

I had owned cats my entire adult life. I had never found a whisker on a pillow.

I told myself I was being dramatic. Cats shed. Whiskers fall out. I threw it away and went to make coffee.

Group obedience class. 6 weeks. $119. Rosie performed perfectly in the classroom. Sat on command. Held a stay. Looked like a trained dog.

Nothing transferred home. The second the doorbell rang, every command disappeared.

Private trainer. $150 a session. 4 sessions. $600. He told me to turn my back when she jumps. I turned my back. She jumped on my back instead. He told me to ignore the behavior. I ignored it for 4 weeks straight.

Nothing.

I looked at board and train programs. Read everything I could find. Then read about the $1,200 price tags and the 2 week results that collapse the day the dog comes home and put my phone down.

I was not spending that kind of money for 2 weeks of peace.

So I tried everything else.

Calming chews for 3 months. CBD oil twice a day for 2 months. An e-collar I used once, heard her yelp, took it off, and threw it in the trash.

Nothing changed.

And here is the worst part.

It started with jumping. Now it had spread to everything. Pulling on the leash so hard I had a permanent callus on my palm.

Selective hearing so severe she wouldn't respond to her own name outside a quiet room.

data.caption: Clean Energy, Sharp Focus
data.copy:
After years of wasting money on supplements that did nothing, the question I get asked most is this: how long does it actually take to notice anything from astaxanthin?

The honest answer is, it depends on how consistent you are and where you're starting from. But once people start taking a proper natural dose every day, most describe a pretty predictable timeline.

In the first 1 to 2 weeks, a lot of folks notice steadier daily energy and less of that fried, tired feeling in their eyes after a long day of screens.

By week 4, the skin tends to catch up. It starts looking a little fresher and less washed out, and the afternoon fog isn't as heavy.

Around 8 weeks, that's when it really stacks. Skin, energy, eyes, and focus all feeling more like they used to, because the support builds up in your cells over time instead of all at once.

That's why I look for the natural, oil-based kind with a full dose, not stimulants and not cheap synthetic powder. Your body responds best to steady support, not a jolt.

This isn't a quick fix. It's daily support for a body that works for you around the clock.

data.caption: Doctor Secret About Nail Fungus They Don't Tell You
data.copy:
I'm a podiatrist. I've been practicing for 11 years. And I need to tell you something we never say in the office about toenail fungus.

Most of what we send you home with cannot reach the fungus.

Not because we don't care.

Because of something so simple it will make you angry.

I see women in my clinic every week who have had this for five, six, eight years. They've tried everything. They come in as a last resort. They sit on my table and show me their feet and I can see what it cost them just to do that.

Some of them haven't shown anyone their feet in years.

Not a friend. Not a partner. No one.

And I run through my options.

Ciclopirox. Jublia. Terbinafine.

I know before I finish the sentence what they're going to say about terbinafine.

The liver panels. The forums. The woman whose hair never came back the same.

I don't blame them.

So I write the topical prescription instead.

And here is what I never say when I hand it over.

The fungus in toenail infections does not live on the surface of the nail. It lives underneath it. In the nail bed. Buried beneath one of the densest structures in the human body.

When you brush a liquid onto the top of your nail and wait for it to dry before putting your sock on, that liquid is in contact with your nail for maybe sixty seconds.

Sixty seconds against a nail plate that was built by millions of years of evolution specifically to keep things out.

It doesn't get through.

Not to where the fungus actually is.

We know this. It is not a secret inside medicine. It is just something nobody explains to the woman sitting across from us holding a prescription she is about to spend $180 on.

I prescribed these things because they were what I had. Because the alternative was telling someone who had driven forty minutes and waited three months for an appointment that I had nothing for her that wouldn't also frighten her.

So I handed over the prescription and moved on to the next patient.

data.caption: This Magnesium Truth Will Make You Furious 👆
data.copy:
Please STOP Taking Magnesium Until You Read This!
 
Because that bottle you bought? It's probably filled with something your body can't even absorb.
 
Let me explain.
 
For two years, I took magnesium every single night before bed. And every single night, I'd snap awake at half past two with my heart doing something strange and my mind already running at full speed.
 
Then I'd lie there for hours. Watching the ceiling. Calculating how exhausted I'd be tomorrow.
 
I was sleeping 3 to 5 hours a night. Broken. Restless. Awful.
 
I tried six different brands. Highly rated on Amazon. Recommended by health bloggers. Some were cheap. Some were expensive. One cost nearly £40 a bottle.
 
Nothing worked. Most of them gave me digestive problems and absolutely nothing else.
 
I kept telling myself: "Maybe magnesium just doesn't work for me."
 
But the sleeplessness wasn't even the worst part.
 
The worst part was watching myself disappear. The patient mum who used to enjoy her grandchildren. The engaged wife. The woman who used to have energy for things she loved.
 
Gone.
 
I felt like my own body had turned against me.
 
My GP's response? "It's quite common at your age, Margaret. Your blood tests look fine. Have you tried melatonin?"
 
Then everything changed at a charity fundraising lunch in Leeds.
 
I was struggling to stay awake by 2 in the afternoon. Started chatting to the woman beside me just to keep myself alert. Turned out she was Dr. Caroline Webb. A sleep specialist with seventeen years of experience, now working privately after years in the NHS.
 
I mentioned my sleep problems almost as a throwaway comment.
 
"Have you tried magnesium?" she asked.
 
I almost laughed out loud. "Six brands. Magnesium does nothing for me except upset my stomach."
 
She gave me a look I'd come to recognise later. The look of someone who'd heard this exact sentence hundreds of times.
 
"Can I ask what you're taking?"
 
I pulled out my phone and showed her my most recent order on Amazon.…

data.caption: Read this if menopause gave you dry mouth ☝️
data.copy:
I have been treating dry mouth for 18 years and I recently noticed one pattern: 90% of the people walking into my office with dry mouth are using a CPAP machine for sleep apnea. When I moved to America, I could not believe what doctors here were telling these patients.

The first 20 of those years were spent practicing in Milan.

2 years ago, my wife's company relocated her to Seattle, so I made the move with her. 

I took a position at a women's health clinic here. Excellent clinic. Skilled clinicians.

Patient after patient, women between 50 and 65, coming through the door with persistent dry mouth. 

Their lips cracked. New cavities appearing for what seemed like no reason. 

Bolting awake at 3am because their tongue was glued to the roof of their mouth.

"My doctor said we are just keeping an eye on it since menopause started."

Keeping an eye on it.

Back in Italy, that is not how we approach this condition. 

We go after the cause. 

Because once you are waking 3 times a night gasping for moisture, something biological has already broken down, and no amount of water sipping is going to undo that.

All it does is push the deterioration further down the road.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
